The zoonotic origin of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains under active investigation. Here, we present a phylogenomic analysis of sarbecovirus genomes recovered from bat, pangolin, and human isolates to reconstruct the evolutionary ancestry of the pandemic strain. Whole-genome sequencing and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 clusters within the SARS-related coronavirus clade, sharing 96.2% genome identity with bat SARS-related coronaviruses (RaTG13). Structural modeling of the receptor-binding domain reveals high affinity for human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), consistent with adaptive evolution. While environmental spillover and intermediate-host transmission remain plausible, our data support a natural zoonotic origin over the laboratory-adjacency hypothesis. These findings refine our understanding of coronavirus emergence and inform surveillance strategies targeting reservoir hosts.

The zoonotic origin of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains a subject of intense investigation. Here, we analyze genomic phylogenetics and bat coronavirus surveillance data from Southeast Asia to evaluate evolutionary trajectories underlying cross-species transmission. Phylogenomic reconstruction of the receptor-binding domain reveals high sequence homology with SARS-related coronaviruses isolated from *Rhinolophus* species, supporting an animal reservoir as the probable progenitor. We further assess the role of intermediate hosts and furin cleavage site acquisition in facilitating human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 entry. Our findings suggest that recombination events within bat populations, coupled with ecological interface exposure, represent the most parsimonious explanatory model for the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, while acknowledging residual uncertainty regarding the precise spillover event.

The zoonotic origin of SARS-CoV-2 remains a subject of intense investigation. Here, we present a phylogenomic analysis of bat and pangolin coronavirus genomes sequenced across Southeast Asia, revealing that RaTG13 and related sarbecoviruses share 96.2% genome-level identity with SARS-CoV-2. Structural modeling of the receptor-binding domain demonstrates high-affinity attachment to human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), with key residues at positions 455, 486, and 501 enhancing binding competence. Recombination analysis identified a polybase site and furin cleavage motif arising through recombination events in an intermediate reservoir. Our findings support a natural zoonotic origin and underscore the surveillance imperative for sarbecoviruses circulating in bat and pangolin populations.

The evolutionary origin of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains under active investigation. Here, we present a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of sarbecovirus genomes to elucidate the zoonotic transmission dynamics underlying the emergence of the pandemic strain. Using maximum-likelihood reconstruction and molecular clock dating, we demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 shares 96.2% genome identity with bat coronaviruses (RaTG13) and 91% with pangolin-derived isolates. Structural modeling of the spike protein receptor-binding domain reveals high-affinity binding to human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), supporting a bat reservoir with potential intermediate hosts. Recombination analysis identifies a polybase cleavage site at the S1/S2 junction, suggesting enhanced fitness. Our findings refine the estimated time of most recent common ancestor to late 2019 and underscore the role of wildlife markets in spillover events.

The evolutionary origin of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains a subject of intense scientific inquiry. Here, we present a phylogenetic and genomic analysis of sarbecoviruses isolated from *Rhinolophus* bat reservoir hosts across Southeast Asia. Whole-genome sequencing and maximum-likelihood reconstruction reveal that SARS-CoV-2 shares 96.2% genome-wide identity with bat coronavirus RaTG13, indicating a likely zoonotic origin mediated by an intermediate animal reservoir. Structural modeling of the receptor-binding domain demonstrates high affinity for the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, consistent with adaptive evolution prior to human spillover. Our findings support natural selection as the primary driver of cross-species transmission, arguing against laboratory-adjacent origins for the index outbreak. These data refine our understanding of coronavirus emergence and inform surveillance strategies targeting reservoir hosts.

The zoonotic origin of SARS-CoV-2 remains a subject of intensive investigation. Here, we present a comprehensive phylogenetic and structural analysis comparing the novel coronavirus genome against reference sequences from bat and pangolin coronaviruses. Our genomic surveillance data indicate that SARS-CoV-2 shares 96.2% nucleotide identity with the bat coronavirus RaTG13, supporting a natural evolutionary origin rather than artificial engineering. Phylogenomic reconstruction places SARS-CoV-2 within the Sarbecovirus genus, with the receptor-binding domain exhibiting high affinity for human ACE2. Environmental sampling of live-animal markets and serological surveys of adjacent human populations suggest an intermediate host may have facilitated the initial zoonotic spillover event. These findings refine current models of coronavirus emergence and inform future pandemic preparedness strategies.

The evolutionary origin of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains a subject of intense scientific inquiry. Here, we present a comprehensive phylogenetic and genomic analysis indicating a zoonotic origin, with bats serving as the primary natural reservoir. Comparative genomics revealed 96% nucleotide identity between SARS-CoV-2 and bat sarbecoviruses (RaTG13), while structural modeling of the receptor-binding domain underscores functional compatibility with human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). We evaluate two principal transmission scenarios: direct spillover from a reservoir host versus intermediate host amplification. Epidemiological and metagenomic evidence from wildlife markets supports the intermediate-host hypothesis, though environmental sampling cannot be excluded. Our findings refine predictive models for future zoonotic surveillance and highlight the importance of monitoring coronavirus diversity in chiropteran populations.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, zoonotic spillover, phylogenetics, bat sarbecovirus, receptor-binding domain

The zoonotic origin of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) remains under active investigation. Here, we performed comprehensive phylogenomic and structural analyses of sarbecoviruses recovered from bat and pangolin reservoirs across Southeast Asia. Our reconstruction of the coronavirus evolutionary tree indicates that SARS-CoV-2 clusters within a clade sharing 96.2% genome identity with bat coronavirus RaTG13. Notably, the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of SARS-CoV-2 exhibits high affinity for human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), with a receptor-binding motif most closely resembling that of pangolin sarbecoviruses. These findings support a natural zoonotic spillover event rather than artificial engineering, though an intermediate animal host likely facilitated human adaptation. Our data refine the evolutionary timeline and identify candidate precursor viruses critical for understanding coronavirus emergence and future pandemic preparedness.

Social distancing measures were deployed globally to mitigate SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This study quantified the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) on epidemic dynamics.

**Methods:** We employed a compartmental SIR model calibrated to reported incidence data across multiple jurisdictions, estimating the effective reproduction number (Rₜ) before and after implementation of social distancing policies.

**Results:** Implementation of social distancing reduced median Rₜ by 42% (95% CI: 38-46%) relative to baseline. Compliance exceeding 70% was associated with a 55% reduction in peak incidence and delayed the epidemic peak by an estimated 18 days, thereby alleviating healthcare system burden.

**Conclusion:** Social distancing substantially reduced SARS-CoV-2 transmission and should be integrated with complementary NPIs during future surges.

Social distancing measures represent a cornerstone of nonpharmaceutical interventions deployed to curb coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) transmission. Using a compartmental susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) model parameterized with estimated baseline reproduction numbers, we quantified the epidemiological impact of varying distancing intensities on incidence and healthcare demand. Simulations demonstrated that sustained 1-meter interpersonal spacing reduced the effective reproduction number below the epidemic threshold by 38–52%, depending on compliance rates, while a 1-meter reduction in contact frequency attenuated peak prevalence by approximately 41%. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the timing of intervention initiation exerted a disproportionately large effect on cumulative infections. Our findings suggest that moderate-to-strong social distancing, when implemented early and maintained with high adherence, substantially mitigates transmission and delays healthcare system overload.

Social distancing interventions have represented a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical measures deployed to mitigate SARS-CoV-2 transmission. Using a compartmental Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) framework parameterized with empirical contact-matrix data, we quantified the effect of reduced interpersonal proximity on the effective reproduction number (Rₑ) across diverse demographic settings. Simulations incorporating a 60% reduction in close-contact frequency yielded a median 47% decline in Rₑ (95% credible interval: 39–54%), substantially delaying the epidemic peak and reducing healthcare-capacity overload by an estimated 38%. Heterogeneity analysis revealed that adherence intensity and duration of intervention were stronger determinants of outcome than physical distance per se. Combined with mask efficacy, sustained social distancing suppressed incidence by up to 62% relative to the baseline scenario. Our findings underscore the necessity of maintaining distancing policies in conjunction with vaccination campaigns to prevent resurgence.

Social distancing interventions represent a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical measures deployed to mitigate SARS-CoV-2 transmission. Using a compartmental Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible (SIRS) model, we estimated the epidemiological impact of varying physical distance protocols on the effective reproduction number (Rₜ) across urban populations. Simulations incorporating contact matrix data demonstrated that sustained maintenance of ≥1 meter separation reduced peak incidence by 34% (95% CI: 28–41%), whereas 2 meter protocols yielded an additional 19% reduction in transmission rate. Sensitivity analysis indicated that compliance adherence, rather than distance per se, exerted the greatest influence on outbreak trajectory. Our findings suggest that layered distancing measures, combined with high compliance, substantially depress Rₜ below the critical threshold of unity, thereby reducing healthcare system burden.

Social distancing interventions represent a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical measures deployed to mitigate transmission of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Using a compartmental susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) framework parameterized with empirical contact-matrix data, we quantified the effect of reduced interpersonal proximity on the effective reproduction number (Rₑ). Simulations incorporating a 50% reduction in social contacts yielded a projected decline in Rₑ of 0.8–1.4 across diverse demographic settings, corresponding to an estimated 42–58% reduction in peak incidence. Sensitivity analyses indicated that sustained adherence over a minimum of twelve weeks was requisite to avert epidemic resurgence upon relaxation. These findings underscore the efficacy of physical distancing in curbing transmission and informing public health policy during pandemic waves.

This study quantified the impact of social distancing interventions on SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics using an age-structured compartmental model calibrated to reported incidence data across multiple jurisdictions. We estimated the effective reproduction number (Rt) under varying degrees of contact reduction and assessed the temporal relationship between policy implementation and epidemic trajectory. Simulations incorporating a 50% reduction in social contacts yielded an estimated 42% decline in peak incidence and a proportional prolongation of the epidemic peak, thereby reducing health system load. Sensitivity analyses indicated that sustained compliance exceeding 60% was requisite to maintain Rt below the critical threshold of 1.0. Our findings demonstrate that non-pharmaceutical social distancing constitutes a pivotal suppressive strategy, with epidemiological benefit directly contingent upon adherence levels and implementation duration.

Social distancing interventions represent a cornerstone of nonpharmaceutical mitigation strategies against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Using a compartmental susceptible-infectious-recovered-removed (SIR) model parametrized with empirical contact-rate data, we quantified the effect of reduced interpersonal proximity on disease transmission dynamics. Our analysis demonstrates that sustained 1-meter distancing combined with reduced contact frequency attenuates the effective reproduction number (Rₜ), achieving an estimated 40–60% reduction in the basic reproduction number (R₀) at community scale. Model projections indicate that compliance rates below 50% substantially diminish population-level impact, yielding prolonged epidemic peaks and increased cumulative incidence. These findings underscore the dose-response relationship between distancing adherence and morbidity burden, informing targeted public health policy.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, nonpharmaceutical interventions, Rₜ, contact rate, epidemic modeling

Social distancing interventions represent a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical measures deployed to mitigate SARS-CoV-2 transmission. Using a compartmental susceptible-infectious-recovered-susceptible (SIRS) model parameterized with empirically derived contact matrices, we quantified the epidemiological impact of varying distancing intensities on the effective reproduction number (Rt) and epidemic peak burden. Simulations indicated that a 50% reduction in social contact attenuated Rt by approximately 42% (95% CI: 38–46%) and delayed and flattened the incidence peak, reducing maximal daily hospitalizations by an estimated 37%. Stratified analyses revealed disproportionately greater efficacy among high-contact age cohorts, consistent with superspreading dynamics. Combined with mask utilization, additive contact reductions yielded sub-threshold Rt (<1) within 14 days under modeled compliance scenarios. These findings underscore that sustained, population-level social distancing substantially curbs transmission and defers healthcare demand, informing time-targeted policy interventions during wave surges.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, sudden surges in severe acute respiratory syndrome cases overwhelmed healthcare infrastructure, necessitating systematic rationing of intensive care unit (ICU) beds, invasive mechanical ventilators, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) resources. We developed a predictive model integrating regional admission rates, occupancy thresholds, and disease severity scores to forecast resource scarcity 72 hours in advance. Applying this framework to three metropolitan health systems (n = 4,812 critical patients), we observed that a utilitarian triage protocol incorporating the SOFA score reduced projected mortality by 14.7% relative to first-come-first-served allocation (95% CI: 9.2–20.1; p < 0.001). Resource exhaustion was delayed by a median of 5.3 days under optimized distribution. Our findings suggest that anticipatory rationing algorithms, combined with transparent ethical criteria, can substantially improve survival outcomes during epidemic peak conditions.

The acute surge in SARS-CoV-2 infections imposed unprecedented strain on healthcare systems, necessitating structured rationing of intensive care unit (ICU) beds and ventilators. **Methods:** We developed a decision-analytic model to evaluate three allocation strategies—triage by SOFA score, by quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and by randomised lottery—across simulated cohorts of 10,000 patients requiring mechanical ventilation. **Results:** SOFA-based prioritisation maximised short-term survival (62.4% discharged) but excluded patients with comorbidities at disproportionate rates, whereas QALY-weighted allocation optimised long-term population health (mean 8.2 QALYs gained per bed) at the cost of intergenerational equity. The lottery approach yielded the most equitable distribution but lowest overall survival (51.1%). **Conclusion:** Context-dependent trade-offs exist between efficiency, equity, and survival, supporting hybrid frameworks incorporating clinical reversibility as a prioritisation criterion.

The acute surge in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) admissions imposed unprecedented strain on healthcare capacity, necessitating structured rationing of intensive care resources. We developed a predictive triage model integrating the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, arterial oxygen tension-to-fragment ratio (PaO₂/FiO₂), and age-stratified comorbidity burden to prioritize mechanical ventilation allocation. Applying this framework to simulated cohort data (n = 4,318) across three regional hospital networks, we estimated that a utility-maximizing allocation protocol increased projected survival by 14.7% (95% CI: 11.2–18.3) relative to first-came, first-served distribution. Multivariate analysis identified respiratory failure onset within 72 hours of admission as the strongest independent predictor of ICU disposition delays. Our findings suggest that transparent, evidence-based rationing criteria can mitigate mortality during capacity crises while preserving clinical equity.

The acute surge in SARS-CoV-2 infections overwhelmed healthcare capacity, necessitating systematic rationing of intensive care resources. We evaluated allocation frameworks for ventilators and intensive care unit (ICU) beds during peak pandemic demand.

Methods: Using a retrospective cohort design across 42 tertiary centres (n = 6,841 critically ill patients), we applied the SOFA-based triage score alongside a modified Yale-OSIA severity index to prioritise resource distribution. Primary outcomes included 28-day mortality and ventilator-free days.

Results: Patients stratified by higher severity scores exhibited markedly increased mortality (OR 3.71, 95% CI 2.88–4.94; p < 0.001). Implementation of protocolised rationing reduced time-to-intubation by 34% and was associated with improved resource utilisation efficiency (β = 0.62, p = 0.003), though overall ICU occupancy exceeded 96% during peak admissions.

Conclusion: Standardised, objective triage criteria optimise rationing outcomes and should inform future surge capacity planning.

The acute surge in severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections imposes critical constraints on intensive care unit (ICU) capacity and mechanical ventilation availability, necessitating structured rationing frameworks. We developed a decision-support model to optimize resource allocation under capacity-constrained conditions, integrating the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score with a comorbidity-adjusted quality-adjusted life year (QALY) weighting scheme. Applying the model to projected ICU demand across a representative tertiary network, we estimated that concurrent surge scenarios could exhaust mechanical ventilation reserves within 72 hours under baseline allocation protocols. Stratified prioritization by predicted survival probability reduced avoidable mortality by an estimated 18.4% (95% CI: 12.1–24.7%) compared with first-come-first-served allocation. Our findings suggest that transparent, evidence-based triage criteria can improve outcomes during resource scarcity while maintaining ethical consistency in allocation decisions.

The disproportionate surge in severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections frequently overwhelms intensive care unit (ICU) capacity, necessitating systematic rationing of scarce resources such as ventilators, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and invasive mechanical ventilation. We developed and validated a predictive triage model integrating clinical, demographic, and laboratory variables to stratify patient prognosis and optimize resource allocation during peak surges. Applying this framework to 4,217 ICU admissions across 12 tertiary centers, our model demonstrated robust discriminative performance (C-statistic 0.82, 95% CI 0.79–0.85) in predicting 28-day mortality. Simulation analyses indicated that algorithm-assisted rationing improved life-years gained by 18.4% relative to conventional first-come-first-served allocation. These findings support the integration of evidence-based, transparent decision-support tools into institutional surge protocols to maximize population-level outcomes during resource-constrained conditions.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, ICU rationing, triage, resource allocation

The rapid surge in severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections imposed unprecedented strain on intensive care unit (ICU) capacity, necessitating systematic rationing of critical resources. We developed a predictive model to optimize allocation of limited ventilators, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) units, and ICU beds across three regional health networks during peak prevalence. Using retrospective clinical data (n = 4,217) collected over a 14-week period, we integrated the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index, and time-series incidence projections to derive triage thresholds. Our algorithm reduced projected mortality among non-admitted severe cases by an estimated 18.4% (95% CI: 12.1–24.9%) relative to standard care protocols, while preserving equity metrics across demographic subgroups. Findings support the implementation of dynamic, evidence-based rationing frameworks to maximize survival outcomes under capacity-constrained conditions.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, surges in severe respiratory failure overwhelmed intensive care unit (ICU) capacity, necessitating structured rationing of scarce resources, including invasive mechanical ventilation and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). We developed and validated a multidisciplinary triage framework integrating the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, arterial oxygenation indices, and comorbidity burden to prioritize allocation. Applying this model to simulated cohort data (N = 4,200), we observed a 23% improvement in life-years saved relative to first-come-first-served protocols, with differential outcomes stratified by age and immunocompromised status. Machine-learning calibration of our scoring algorithm reduced ethical disagreements among clinicians by 31%. Our findings suggest that transparent, criterion-based rationing protocols can optimize resource utilization while maintaining distributive justice during acute capacity constraints.

The implementation of quarantine protocols represents a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical interventions during coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemics. We evaluated the epidemiological efficacy of mandatory home quarantine policies across 14 metropolitan regions using a compartmental Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model calibrated with confirmed case and mortality data spanning March–June 2020. Quarantine compliance was estimated from mobility datasets and incorporated as a time-varying transmission reduction parameter. Our results indicate that sustained quarantine adherence of ≥78% attenuated the effective reproduction number (Rₑ) to 0.6–0.9, corresponding to a 41% reduction (95% CI: 33–49%) in peak incidence compared with unmitigated scenarios. Notably, delayed initiation of quarantine beyond 21 days post-intervention was associated with a 2.3-fold increase in cumulative mortality. These findings underscore the temporal sensitivity of quarantine measures and support early, high-compliance enforcement to mitigate healthcare system burden.

The effectiveness of quarantine as a non-pharmaceutical intervention in mitigating SARS-CoV-2 transmission remains a critical determinant of pandemic control. Here, we analyzed the impact of varying quarantine durations and compliance rates on the effective reproduction number (Rt) using a compartmental SEIR model parameterized with clinical and contact-tracing data. Our results demonstrate that a 14-day self-isolation protocol, combined with contact tracing, reduced peak incidence by 47% relative to baseline. Sensitivity analyses indicated that compliance rates below 60% substantially attenuated intervention efficacy, driving Rt above the epidemic threshold of unity. These findings underscore the necessity of sustained adherence and recommend integrating quarantine with molecular surveillance to optimize resource allocation during elevated community transmission.

Quarantine remains a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical intervention strategies during SARS-CoV-2 pandemics, yet the optimal duration and compliance dynamics remain contested. We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis (N = 14,283) to evaluate the efficacy of 14-day versus 7-day home quarantine combined with a single SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid test. Using a compartmental transmission model parameterized with real-world contact-tracing data, we estimated the attributable fraction of secondary infections. Results indicated that 7-day quarantine with a negative test reduced onward transmission by 71.4% (95% CI: 66.8–75.9%) relative to the standard 14-day protocol, with no statistically significant difference in delayed cases (p = 0.082). Compliance rates declined precipitously after day 7 (OR = 0.43). Our findings support shortened quarantine protocols to balance epidemiological effectiveness with socioeconomic sustainability.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, quarantine, non-pharmaceutical interventions, transmission dynamics

Non-pharmaceutical interventions, particularly quarantine of SARS-CoV-2 contacts, remain central to epidemic containment. We quantified the effectiveness of varying quarantine durations in reducing secondary transmission.

Methods: Using a compartmental epidemiological model calibrated to confirmed case data, we simulated quarantine periods of 7 versus 14 days under conditions of pre-symptomatic infectiousness and test-to-release strategies.

Results: A 7-day quarantine with a negative nucleic acid amplification test (NAT) at day 5 reduced secondary attack risk by 63% (95% CI: 57–69%), approaching the 71% (95% CI: 66–76%) reduction achieved by 14-day isolation. Benefit was substantially attenuated among index cases with prolonged viral shedding.

Conclusion: Shortened quarantine coupled with molecular testing offers a cost-effective alternative to standard 14-day isolation, balancing epidemiological efficacy against socioeconomic burden during periods of high transmissibility.

This study evaluated the effectiveness of quarantine interventions in mitigating transmission of SARS-CoV-2 during the initial wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a compartmental Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model parameterized with epidemiological surveillance data from multiple geographic regions, we estimated the reduction in effective reproduction number (Rt) associated with varying quarantine durations and adherence rates. Simulations indicated that 14-day quarantine protocols reduced peak incidence by 42–58% relative to no intervention, with compliance exceeding 75% yielding the greatest population-level impact. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that quarantine efficacy was most sensitive to the proportion of asymptomatic transmission. These findings underscore the critical role of sustained quarantine adherence in attenuating healthcare burden and inform evidence-based non-pharmaceutical intervention strategies.

Quarantine remains a cornerstone of non-pharmaceutical intervention strategies for controlling severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) transmission. We developed a compartmental Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Quarantined (SIRQ) model to quantify the effectiveness of targeted quarantine protocols relative to community-wide restrictions. Using incidence data from three high-burden regions, we estimated the effective reproduction number (Rₜ) under varying quarantine compliance rates and isolation latency intervals. Our analysis demonstrated that quarantine implemented within 5 days of symptom onset, combined with ≥80% contact tracing compliance, reduced peak incidence by 47% (95% CI: 39–54%) and shortened the epidemic plateau by an estimated 21 days. Delayed isolation beyond 7 days attenuated this benefit by 31%. These findings underscore the critical dependence of quarantine efficacy on surveillance speed and population adherence, informing resource allocation during future respiratory viral surges.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, quarantine, contact tracing, epidemiological modeling

Quarantine represents a cornerstone of nonpharmacological intervention during respiratory pandemic responses. We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis to quantify the effect of mandated quarantine protocols on SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics across 14 metropolitan regions during the initial wave of the pandemic. Using a difference-in-differences estimator applied to confirmed case incidence, contact-tracing data, and mobility metrics over a 90-day surveillance window, we estimated the relative reduction in the effective reproduction number (Rₜ). Stratified regression models adjusted for demographic density, comorbidity prevalence, and testing capacity. Our findings indicate that compliance-adherent quarantine periods of ≥14 days reduced community transmission by 41% (95% CI: 33–48%) relative to shorter isolation intervals. These results support extended quarantine durations as an effective epidemiological control measure, particularly in high-density urban settings.

The efficacy of quarantine protocols in mitigating coronavirus transmission remains a central public health priority. We employed a compartmental Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model, integrated with contact-tracing data, to quantify the impact of mandatory home quarantine on the effective reproduction number (Rt) across diverse population densities. Our analysis of 14-week surveillance datasets (n = 248,563 cases) demonstrated that quarantine durations of 14 days, initiated within 48 hours of exposure, reduced secondary attack rates by 61% (95% CI: 54–68%) relative to no intervention. Sensitivity analyses indicated that compliance adherence and the proportion of asymptomatic transmission were the dominant determinants of overall effectiveness. These findings support the integration of extended quarantine periods with rapid diagnostic screening to optimize resource allocation during respiratory viral outbreaks.

**Keywords:** coronavirus, quarantine, epidemiology, SEIR modeling, transmission dynamics

Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) primarily propagates through respiratory routes following binding of its spike glycoprotein to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors on host cells. The dominant transmission pathway is direct deposition of respiratory droplets generated during speaking, coughing, or sneezing, with particle size (1–100 µm) determining deposition depth within the respiratory tract. Increasing evidence indicates that submicron aerosols facilitate prolonged airborne dissemination, particularly in poorly ventilated enclosed environments. Contact transmission via fomites remains possible, though its relative contribution is comparatively limited. Viral load in upper respiratory secretions correlates positively with transmissibility, with the presymptomatic and asymptomatic periods contributing substantially to silent spread. Understanding these mechanisms informs nonpharmaceutical interventions, including masking, ventilation, and social distancing strategies.

**Keywords:** SARS-CoV-2, droplet transmission, aerosols, ACE2, respiratory pathogen

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is transmitted between humans predominantly through respiratory routes. The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) initiates infection by binding the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, highly expressed in respiratory epithelium. Transmission occurs chiefly via large respiratory droplets expelled during coughing, sneezing, and phonation. Infectious aerosols containing viable viral particles additionally enable airborne spread, especially within poorly ventilated indoor environments. Direct contact with contaminated fomites, followed by self-inoculation of the conjunctiva, nasal, or oral mucosa, represents a secondary fomite-mediated route. Notably, pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals sustain transmission owing to elevated presymptomatic viral load. These mechanistic insights underpin non-pharmaceutical interventions, including mask efficacy, environmental ventilation standards, and social distancing protocols.

This study characterizes the transmission dynamics of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the etiological agent of COVID-19. We examine principal spread routes, emphasizing respiratory droplet and aerosol-mediated transmission. The virus enters host cells via angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, predominantly expressed in respiratory epithelium. Direct person-to-person transmission occurs through inhalation of infectious respiratory aerosols generated by infected individuals during speaking, coughing, or breathing. Larger droplets facilitate short-range spread, while submicron aerosols enable prolonged airborne suspension and longer-range dissemination. Fomite transmission via contaminated surfaces contributes to secondary infection routes. The basic reproduction number (R₀) and superspreading events underscore the role of human behavior and environmental conditions in modulating transmission efficiency, thereby informing targeted public health interventions.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) disseulates primarily through respiratory aerosols and droplets. The principal transmission route involves airborne deposition of virion-laden nuclei emitted during respiration, speech, and coughing, with sustained suspension of sub-micron aerosols enabling long-range inhalational exposure. Direct and indirect contact transmission further propagates infection via deposition of infectious particles on mucosal surfaces of the conjunctiva, nasal mucosa, and oropharynx, followed by receptor-mediated cellular entry through the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) transmembrane protease. Fomite-mediated transfer of viable virions across high-touch surfaces contributes to secondary transmission, particularly in enclosed, poorly ventilated environments. Our analysis demonstrates that transmission intensity correlates significantly with cumulative viral load, ventilation rate, and interpersonal proximity, underscoring the multifactorial nature of coronavirus spread.

This study characterizes the transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19. We evaluate multiple routes of human-to-human spread, including large respiratory droplet deposition, inhalation of aerosolized virions in enclosed and poorly ventilated environments, and contact with contaminated surfaces (fomite transmission). Viral entry is initiated by spike glycoprotein binding to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors expressed on respiratory epithelial cells. We demonstrate that superspreading events correlate with elevated viral load, prolonged exposure duration, and inadequate ventilation. Pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals contribute substantially to community spread owing to presymptomatic viral shedding. Our findings underscore the efficacy of layered mitigation strategies—respiratory masking, improved ventilation, and physical distancing—in reducing the effective reproduction number (Rₑ), thereby informing targeted public health interventions.

SARS-CoV-2 primarily propagates through respiratory routes, with person-to-person transmission mediated by respiratory droplets and aerosols generated during breathing, speaking, coughing, and singing. Larger droplets (>5 µm) deposit on mucosal surfaces of the conjunctiva, nasal mucosa, and oropharynx, whereas submicron aerosols facilitate long-range airborne dissemination, particularly in poorly ventilated indoor environments. Secondary transmission occurs via fomites, in which viable virions persist on high-touch surfaces and are transferred to facial mucosa through hand contact. Viral load in respiratory secretions, peak approximately two days before symptom onset, underscores the substantial role of presymptomatic and asymptomatic spread. Environmental factors—including reduced relative humidity, lower temperature, and diminished ventilation—enhance aerosol stability and accumulation. Understanding these multipathway dissemination mechanisms informs non-pharmaceutical interventions, including mask efficacy, social distancing, and airborne infection control strategies.

The viral spike protein mediates cellular entry by binding the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, with high viral loads in the upper respiratory tract facilitating efficient person-to-person spread. Evidence indicates that aerosols persist and accumulate in poorly ventilated indoor environments, enabling transmission over distances exceeding one metre. Direct contact with contaminated fomites, followed by self-inoculation of mucous membranes, contributes to a lesser extent. Superspreading events, elevated by high transmissibility during the presymptomatic phase, substantially amplify community-level dissemination. These findings underscore the utility of improved ventilation, respiratory protection, and source control as effective mitigation strategies.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) dissemits primarily through respiratory routes, with person-to-person transmission mediated by respiratory droplets and aerosolized particles expelled during breathing, speaking, coughing, and sneezing. The virus initiates infection via binding of its spike glycoprotein to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors expressed on respiratory epithelial cells. Evidence indicates that both large droplet deposition and fine aerosol suspension contribute to spread, with the latter facilitating transmission over extended distances, particularly in poorly ventilated indoor environments. Additionally, contact with contaminated surfaces (fomite transmission) may contribute to infection through mucosal entry. Viral load, measured by cycle threshold values, correlates with infectiousness, underscoring the significance of asymptomatic and presymptomatic individuals in sustaining community transmission dynamics.

Superspreaders and superspreading events account for a disproportionate fraction of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) transmissions, yet the underlying virological and behavioral determinants remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed contact-tracing data from three epidemiological waves (N = 4,312 index cases) to quantify the dispersion parameter *k* and associated reproduction number heterogeneity. Using multivariable negative binomial regression, we identified elevated nasopharyngeal viral load, prolonged indoor exposure, and respiratory density as independent predictors of transmission superspreading. Our estimates indicate that approximately 10–20% of infected individuals generate 80% of secondary cases, with *k* values of 0.14 (95% CI: 0.09–0.21). These findings underscore the pivotal role of stochastic, context-dependent transmission and support targeted nonpharmaceutical interventions, including ventilation standards and mass testing, to mitigate concentrated outbreak risk.

Superspreaders constitute a disproportionate fraction of SARS-CoV-2 transmissions, yet the individual and contextual determinants of this heterogeneity remain incompletely characterized.
